The rates nobody publishes

6 rates

Where a vendor puts a rate behind a slider, a calculator widget or another company’s pricing page, there is no figure to record. Each of these is why a total involving that service refuses to resolve.

Get told when one of these moves

Every plan here is re-read nightly against the vendor’s own pricing page. When one of them changes, this is the list that hears about it.

Stored so a price change has somewhere to go. Nothing else.

Three rules decide every figure

None of them is a judgement call, and all three are the reason a total sometimes refuses to appear at all.

A plan that cannot carry the usage is not an option

01

A plan with an allowance and no meter to charge overage is hard-capped by construction — there is nothing to buy. So an outgrown free tier is excluded before price is compared at all, and a tier barred from commercial use is excluded outright rather than winning on price.

Unknown is never zero

02

If a plan needs a rate the vendor does not publish, and the usage genuinely exceeds what the plan includes, the total is withheld and the reason is printed in its place. A confident wrong figure is worse than no figure, because you cannot tell it is wrong.

Drift is flagged, never quietly patched

03

Each figure was stored with the literal strings that must still appear on the vendor's page. When the nightly re-read cannot find them, the row is marked as drifted and its verification date stops advancing. Nothing rewrites a price on its own.

What a vendor’s pricing page cannot tell you

A pricing page is written by the vendor, covers only that vendor, and is undated. Those three things are the whole gap.

Questions worth asking

Where do these prices come from?

Each one was read off the vendor's own pricing page and stored with its source URL and with the literal strings that must still appear on that page for the figure to hold.

Nothing is scraped into a number automatically, and nothing is estimated from a press release or another comparison site.

How do you know they are still right?

A job re-fetches all 29 pricing pages every night and re-checks the 139 stored strings. If one is gone, the row is marked as drifted and its verification date stops moving.

It never rewrites a price. A comparison site that silently corrects itself is one you cannot audit, so a changed page becomes a flag rather than a new number.

Why does the total sometimes refuse to appear?

Because a rate that decides it is not published anywhere. Firebase defers to Google Cloud pricing above 50,000 monthly active users; Auth0 puts its MAU steps behind a slider; Stytch's overage rate exists only inside a calculator widget on the page.

In every one of those cases the honest output is that there is no figure. Filling the gap with a zero is how a calculator reports $0 for 100,000 users, which is the specific bug this rule exists to prevent.

What usage do the figures assume?

An ordinary subscription web app: 2% of users paying $20 a month, 30% of revenue taken on international cards, and database, storage, egress and request volumes that scale with the user count. Every one of those assumptions is printed under the calculator.

They are assumptions, not measurements of your app, which is why the arithmetic is shown line by line rather than only as a total.

Is StackTab paid, and are these affiliate links?

No to both. There is no account, no checkout and no per-vendor referral link anywhere on the site. A ranking that earns a commission on the winner is not a ranking.

Free, no account, nothing to sign up for. Change four chips and read the bill at the scale you expect to reach.

Three rules decide every figure

None of them is a judgement call, and all three are the reason a total sometimes refuses to appear at all.

A plan that cannot carry the usage is not an option

01

A plan with an allowance and no meter to charge overage is hard-capped by construction — there is nothing to buy. So an outgrown free tier is excluded before price is compared at all, and a tier barred from commercial use is excluded outright rather than winning on price.

Unknown is never zero

02

If a plan needs a rate the vendor does not publish, and the usage genuinely exceeds what the plan includes, the total is withheld and the reason is printed in its place. A confident wrong figure is worse than no figure, because you cannot tell it is wrong.

Drift is flagged, never quietly patched

03

Each figure was stored with the literal strings that must still appear on the vendor's page. When the nightly re-read cannot find them, the row is marked as drifted and its verification date stops advancing. Nothing rewrites a price on its own.

What a vendor’s pricing page cannot tell you

A pricing page is written by the vendor, covers only that vendor, and is undated. Those three things are the whole gap.

Questions worth asking

Where do these prices come from?

Each one was read off the vendor's own pricing page and stored with its source URL and with the literal strings that must still appear on that page for the figure to hold.

Nothing is scraped into a number automatically, and nothing is estimated from a press release or another comparison site.

How do you know they are still right?

A job re-fetches all 29 pricing pages every night and re-checks the 139 stored strings. If one is gone, the row is marked as drifted and its verification date stops moving.

It never rewrites a price. A comparison site that silently corrects itself is one you cannot audit, so a changed page becomes a flag rather than a new number.

Why does the total sometimes refuse to appear?

Because a rate that decides it is not published anywhere. Firebase defers to Google Cloud pricing above 50,000 monthly active users; Auth0 puts its MAU steps behind a slider; Stytch's overage rate exists only inside a calculator widget on the page.

In every one of those cases the honest output is that there is no figure. Filling the gap with a zero is how a calculator reports $0 for 100,000 users, which is the specific bug this rule exists to prevent.

What usage do the figures assume?

An ordinary subscription web app: 2% of users paying $20 a month, 30% of revenue taken on international cards, and database, storage, egress and request volumes that scale with the user count. Every one of those assumptions is printed under the calculator.

They are assumptions, not measurements of your app, which is why the arithmetic is shown line by line rather than only as a total.

Is StackTab paid, and are these affiliate links?

No to both. There is no account, no checkout and no per-vendor referral link anywhere on the site. A ranking that earns a commission on the winner is not a ranking.
